summary: This experimental document describes the design of a ping protocol for Information-Centric Networking, including how the client and forwarder operate. It is a product of the Information-Centric Networking Research Group.

eli5.summary: Ping says "hello, are you there?" and waits for "yes!" This version works in networks where you ask for things by name, not by address.

subtitle: Test reachability and measure latency in name-based networks.

tldr.problem: IP networks use ping to test whether a host is reachable and to measure round-trip time. Information-Centric Networking (ICN) routes by name instead of address, so network operators need a ping-like tool to test reachability of names and measure latency in the network.
tldr.mechanism: ICN Ping sends Echo Request packets to a name prefix and waits for Echo Reply packets from forwarders or applications that serve that name. The client records the time and computes round-trip time. Forwarders generate replies when they match the request to their administrative name, a cached object, or a local application.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can test the reachability of named data and forwarders, discover which forwarder or cache serves the data, measure round-trip time, and compute loss rates. This aids troubleshooting and understanding ICN deployment.

facts.label: Reply codes
facts.value: 1 for forwarder, 2 for application, 3 for cache hit

today: RFC 9508 is an Experimental protocol published in March 2024 by the Information-Centric Networking Research Group. It represents the consensus of ICNRG on ping design for ICN networks. As an experimental RFC, it may evolve as the ICN community continues deployment and real-world testing.

sections.title: From IP Ping to ICN Ping
sections.content:
In IP networks, the ping utility lets administrators test reachability to a destination host and measure the round-trip time (RTT) of messages. The ping client sends ICMP Echo Request packets with the target IP address as the destination. If the target is reachable, it responds with an ICMP Echo Reply, and the client calculates RTT and loss rate.

Information-Centric Networking (ICN) operates on a different principle: networks route by name prefix, not by IP address. Data sources (applications, caches, repositories) are identified by their published names, not by unique endpoints. This RFC defines an ICN Ping protocol that brings the same troubleshooting capability to name-based networks. ICN Ping tests whether a name is reachable, discovers which forwarder or cache serves it, and measures latency.
sections.eli5: In the old network, you ask a computer "are you there?" In ICN, you ask a name "is anyone publishing you?" and wait to see who responds.

sections.title: IP Ping and ICN Differences
sections.content:
In IP networks, a ping client takes an IP address as input and sends ICMP Echo Request packets with the IP destination address set to the target and the IP source address set to the client's host. Each Echo Request is forwarded across the network based on its destination IP address. If it reaches the target, the target responds by sending an ICMP Echo Reply back to the source IP address. The client measures the time between sending the request and receiving the reply.

ICN networks differ in four major ways. First, ICN names are variable-length hierarchical strings; a single name can refer to data held by multiple sources. Second, ICN Interests (requests) carry no source address; replies follow the reverse path of the Interest based on hop-by-hop state. Third, ICN supports multi-path, multi-destination forwarding; consecutive Interests for the same name can be forwarded along different paths and reach different data sources. Fourth, multiple Interests with the same name arriving at a forwarder are often aggregated in the PIT, so only one request is forwarded onward.

The RFC defines goals for ICN Ping: test the reachability and operational state of ICN forwarders, test whether a producer or cache serves a prefix, discover which forwarder has local connectivity to a producer or cache, and measure RTT and loss rate.
sections.eli5: IP ping asks "are you there?" and waits for "yes." ICN ping asks "who is serving this name?" Ping in ICN is harder because names are not addresses, many sources answer, and requests get merged together.

sections.title: Packet Formats for CCNx and NDN
sections.content:
The RFC defines ping for two ICN implementations: CCNx and Named Data Networking (NDN).

For CCNx, a Ping Echo Request is a special packet type (PT_ECHO_REQUEST) with a hop limit and a Path Label TLV (for path steering, from RFC 9531). The request message carries a name TLV consisting of the prefix to be pinged, appended with a nonce typed name segment. The nonce is a unique 64-bit value to prevent Interest aggregation and allow clients to match replies to requests. Clients can optionally exclude Content Store hits by including a Content Object Hash Restriction TLV with value zero.

A Ping Echo Reply (PT_ECHO_REPLY) looks like a Content Object and includes a Path Label TLV and a payload containing the sender's (forwarder's or application's) name, their signature, and an Echo Reply Code: 1 for forwarder administrative name match, 2 for application prefix match, or 3 for Content Store object match. The reply includes an ExpiryTime TLV set to zero, instructing forwarders not to cache it.

For NDN, a Ping Echo Request is an Interest packet with the target name, the suffix "ping" appended as a KeywordNameComponent, a Nonce field, and a MustBeFresh constraint. The Echo Reply is a Data packet with a FreshnessPeriod of 1 to prevent caching. Both CCNx and NDN formats include the Path Label TLV to enable path steering.
sections.eli5: A ping request is a special packet that says "tell me who you are." A reply says "I am a forwarder named X" or "I am a cache holding this object." The nonce ensures the reply matches the request.

sections.title: Forwarder Operation and Client Behavior
sections.content:
When a forwarder receives an Echo Request, it extracts the base name (the request name without the Nonce segment and the "ping" suffix). The forwarder generates and sends an Echo Reply in three cases: if the base name exactly matches any of the forwarder's administrative names, if the base name exactly matches a Content Object in the Content Store (unless the client excluded CS hits), or if the base name matches a longest-name-prefix in the FIB with an outgoing face to a local application.

If none of these conditions are met, the forwarder attempts to forward the Echo Request upstream based on the FIB LNPM lookup and PIT creation. When a forwarder generates an Echo Reply, it includes the forwarder's own name and signature and the appropriate Echo Reply Code. The reply includes a Path Label TLV with an initial null value. On the reverse path, each forwarder updates the Path Label to encode its next-hop choice.

A ping client application generates Echo Requests and processes Echo Replies. For each new Echo Request, the client generates a new nonce and records the transmission time. The client sets a timeout and waits for the reply. If the reply arrives within the timeout, the client computes RTT as the round-trip time and decodes the Echo Reply Code. When the first Echo Request is sent, it typically includes no Path Label. After receiving a reply with a Path Label, subsequent requests can include that Path Label to steer requests towards the same path for consistent RTT measurements.
sections.eli5: The forwarder checks if the name matches its own name, a cached object, or a local app. If yes, it replies. Otherwise, it forwards the request. The client sends requests, times them, and learns which forwarder serves the name.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Issues
sections.content:
A reflection attack could occur if a compromised forwarder includes the name of a victim forwarder in its Echo Reply, directing future traffic to the victim. To prevent this, forwarders must sign the name included in the reply payload, allowing clients to verify the signature with the forwarder's public key.

An on-path attack could involve a compromised forwarder modifying a reply message to replace the original forwarder's name and signature. To foil such attacks, a forwarder can sign the entire reply message, though this adds computation cost and risk of denial-of-service attacks.

Another attack is the ICN equivalent of port knocking: an attacker sends ping requests to discover forwarder implementations and then attempts to exploit known vulnerabilities.

Interest flooding attacks can be amplified in the second approach to locally scoped namespaces (prepending a routable prefix). A border forwarder must maintain extra state to rewrite reply names when attached to multiple network regions, which could be exploited to create state exhaustion attacks.

Echo Requests have the same privacy characteristics as regular Interests: observers can see that a client is pinging a name, but not the client's identity (since Interests carry no source address).
sections.eli5: Bad actors could pretend to be a forwarder or try to trick the client into sending traffic to the wrong place. Signatures verify who really sent the reply.
